Alright, let's set the scene.

The Senate is a baseball game. The visiting team (the minority party) is losing by a run in the late innings. The home team (the majority) just needs to record the final three outs to pass their bill into law. The manager strolls to the mound to make a pitching change, signaling for the closer. That’s the cloture vote.

The rulebook is very specific: you cannot roll out the tarp until the rain is officially "sustained." So, the Senator has to keep the rain falling. The majority leader, standing in the dugout, is fuming. He’s got a Doppler radar pulled up on his phone, but the radar is just a C-SPAN call-in screen showing the vote count. He needs 60 groundskeepers to vote to roll out the tarp. He’s only got 52. The rain keeps falling. The pitcher is getting cold. The infield is turning into a Slip 'N Slide. The rules of physics (and the Senate) state that a game cannot resume until the downpour stops, but the minority is performing a literal rain dance, and they’ve got bladders of steel.

The rain delay is no longer about wet dirt. The Senator is still talking, but the stadium has entered a temporal anomaly. The rules require the groundskeeper to wait for a "dry track," but the Senator’s voice has actually altered the relative humidity of the chamber to 100%. The microphone is sweating. The lights flicker.
